title: Conway's 99-Graph
tagline: $1,000 prize. 55 years. No one knows if this graph exists.
description: Find a strongly regular graph srg(99, 14, 1, 2): 99 vertices, each with 14 neighbors, where adjacent pairs share exactly 1 common neighbor and non-adjacent pairs share exactly 2. Or prove it cannot exist.
context: Conway offered $1,000 for a construction or impossibility proof. The parameters pass every known necessary condition — integrality, Krein, absolute bound — yet no one has built the graph or ruled it out. The graph cannot be vertex-transitive, which kills all standard algebraic constructions. If it exists, it has to be found by search. The prize was never claimed before Conway's death in 2020.

warmup.title: Warm-up: srg(9, 4, 1, 2)
warmup.body: The Paley graph of order 9 satisfies the same constraints at smaller scale: 9 vertices, degree 4, lambda=1, mu=2. It is unique up to isomorphism. The adjacency matrix below is one representation.

leaderboard.note: The (1,2)-SRG family: all parameter sets with lambda=1, mu=2

verification: Checks: symmetric, zero diagonal, every row sums to 14, A^2 matches lambda/mu conditions for all pairs. Milliseconds.

howToStart.title: Study the 9-vertex case
howToStart.body: Verify the warm-up matrix satisfies srg(9,4,1,2). This builds intuition for the constraint structure.

howToStart.title: Constraint propagation
howToStart.body: Assign edges incrementally. After each, propagate degree-14 and common-neighbor constraints. Most partial assignments contradict quickly.

howToStart.title: SAT / CSP encoding
howToStart.body: 4851 binary variables (upper triangle). Constraints: row sums = 14, A^2 values forced. Modern SAT solvers handle millions of clauses.

howToStart.title: Simulated annealing
howToStart.body: Start with a random 14-regular graph. Score = number of pairs violating lambda/mu. Flip edges to reduce violations.

bounds.name: Not vertex-transitive
bounds.formula: Rules out Paley, Latin square, and most algebraic constructions

bounds.name: All conditions pass
bounds.formula: k(k-lambda-1) = (v-k-1)*mu = 168. Krein and absolute bound satisfied.

references: Biggs, N.L. (1971). Finite Groups of Automorphisms.
